1.how: This was the first data step. The inputs were the SpaceRanger outputs for ten 10x Visium sections, one folder per section. SpaceRanger is the 10x software that turns sequencing reads into a gene-by-spot count table. The unit is the Visium spot, a 55 µm circle that captures RNA from roughly 1 to 10 cells. For each folder the notebook read the filtered count matrix with Scanpy, using gene symbols made unique. It then joined the spot position file, accepting either of two file names because the format varied between runs. Pixel coordinates went into the spatial slot. The image scale factors and high-resolution image were stored with each section. One AnnData file was written per section; AnnData is a Python container for counts plus spot and gene metadata. Nothing was predicted or compared. No quality control was applied and no treatment labels were attached, as those come in §3. There was no formal check, because this step only reformats data.
1.results: The notebook printed ten saved files. P24215_101, P24215_201 and P24215_301 come from one Visium slide. P28052_102, 103, 201, 202, 203, 301 and 401 come from the other. These ten sections are the replicates for the whole project. The files were written to a hard-coded absolute path on the author's other computer, not into this repository. So the step cannot be rerun from the repo as it stands. The catalogue records no spot or gene counts at this stage; those first appear after merging in §2. Two problems were noted. Input and output paths live outside the repo, and no quality control was done. The slide split is already visible in the sample names: three sections on P24215 and seven on P28052. Later runs show this split is confounded with treatment, which became the study's main limitation. No later correction changes what this step produced.

2.how: The inputs were the ten per-section files from §1, still at spot level. The notebook stacked all sections into one AnnData object with an outer join. An outer join keeps a gene even if it is missing from some sections. Each spot barcode got a section suffix, so barcodes from different sections cannot collide. The per-section image metadata was rebuilt, so each section keeps its own image and scale factors. The spatial coordinates were reset to pixel column then pixel row. This fixed an axis flip noted in the logbook, where tissue would otherwise plot rotated or mirrored. The combined object holds raw counts only. As a check, the notebook drew Snap25 on one section and Plp1 on every section. Snap25 marks neurons, and Plp1 marks oligodendrocyte-rich white matter. If the coordinates were wrong, these known anatomical patterns would look flipped or scrambled. Correct-looking maps therefore rule out an orientation error.
2.results: The notebook printed that spatial metadata was harmonised and that the combined file was written. Plp1 maps were rendered for all ten sections. They are the visual evidence that the orientation fix worked. Project memory notes describe the output, combined_samples.h5ad, as 25,671 spots by 19,465 genes of raw counts. These sizes come from the memory notes, not from printed notebook output. The same notes say the file now exists only on the remote analysis machine. So the merged object is not in the repository. Two problems were found. The output path is hard-coded outside the repo. The axis convention is documented only in a code comment, not in the notebook text. No statistics were computed here, so there is nothing to confirm or refute. No later correction targets this step.

3.how: The input was the merged raw-count object from §2, at spot level. Spots with fewer than 200 detected genes were dropped, as were genes seen in fewer than 3 spots. Raw counts were saved in a separate layer for later count-based models. Each spot was then scaled to 10,000 total counts and log-transformed, so deep and shallow spots become comparable. PCA, which compresses thousands of genes into a few summary axes, was run on all genes. Highly variable gene selection and scaling were commented out. A 15-nearest-neighbour graph on 30 components fed UMAP, a 2D similarity map, and Leiden clustering at resolution 0.5. Leiden groups spots with similar expression into clusters. Treatment was added from a hard-coded section-to-treatment dictionary. There was no batch correction and no quantitative check. The only output was a UMAP coloured by cluster and by section. Such a plot shows whether sections mix or separate.
3.results: The object that later notebooks read has 25,660 spots and 18,751 genes. Compared with the merged object from §2, filtering removed about 11 spots and 714 genes. The stored labels give 1 WT section (P24215_101) and 3 BRICHOS sections (P24215_201, P24215_301, P28052_401). The other six P28052 sections are PBS. The dictionary also lists a P24215_401 as PBS, a section that does not exist. Nothing maps to it, so it is harmless, but it misrecords the design. The README describes 1, 3 and 3 mice per group, while the code has 1, 6 and 3 sections. No section-to-mouse mapping exists, so every later replicate is a section, not an animal. **Treatment is fully confounded with slide.** All PBS sections are on P28052, and two of three BRICHOS sections share P24215 with WT. With no batch correction, the global UMAP and clusters mix slide and treatment effects. Notebooks 03/12 to 03/17 later showed the slide effect is large enough to mimic treatment effects.

4.how: The input was the processed object from §3, with one row per spot. A collaborator, Cloé, had drawn brain regions by hand. She exported them as CSV files linking each spot barcode to a region name. The notebook read every CSV and added the section ID from the file name to each barcode. It then matched these barcodes to the spots. Region names were spelled inconsistently between files, for example two versions of "Cortex Layers 2/3/4". A mapping table merged these variants into one vocabulary. Regions were plotted on the UMAP and on each section, and the labelled object was saved. Nothing was tested. The point was to give spots anatomical labels, because the project asks in which brain regions BRICHOS acts. The only check was visual. If barcodes were matched to the wrong section, regions would land in the wrong places on the tissue maps.
4.results: The notebook printed that 17,613 spots received a region label. That leaves about 8,050 of the 25,660 spots unlabelled. Labels included cortical layer groups, caudoputamen, striatum, corpus callosum, hippocampus, hypothalamus, thalamus and amygdala. There were also septal nucleus, ventricular areas, olfactory and optical regions, and an "Excluded" class. The annotation files now in the repository cover only the seven P28052 sections. That fits the partial coverage: the WT section and both P24215 BRICHOS sections seem to lack manual labels. The labels were also drawn differently between sections, for example cortical layers grouped in different ways. A leftover variable built from only the last file is unused. Because of the gaps and inconsistency, these labels were replaced by cluster-derived regions in §8. Later regional analyses mostly use those cluster regions. One exception is a BRICHOS dotplot in §9 that still filters on these manual labels.

5.how: The input was the processed spot-level object from §3, covering all ten sections. The aim was a sanity check: does the APP-NLGF model show its expected plaque-associated glial signature compared with WT? The notebook first showed cluster composition per treatment and marker genes per cluster and per treatment. It then computed a plaque-induced gene (PIG) score per spot from 25 genes such as Apoe, Trem2, Cst7, C1q and C3. A module score is a spot's average expression of the gene set minus that of random control genes with similar expression. A 14-gene oligodendrocyte score (Plp1, Mbp, Mobp and others) was computed the same way. PBS and WT spots were compared with a Mann-Whitney U test, which asks whether one group's values tend to be higher. There was no control for section or slide. Every spot counted as an independent sample. That is pseudoreplication, because spots from the same section share that section's biology and handling.
5.results: The Mann-Whitney test of PIG score, PBS against WT, printed p = 0.0000e+00. That means the p-value fell below floating-point precision. Violin plots show the PIG and oligodendrocyte scores by treatment. No numbers were printed for BRICHOS or for the oligodendrocyte score. BRICHOS was not tested against PBS here. The tiny p-value is not trustworthy as stated. Thousands of spots were treated as independent, but there is only one WT section against six PBS sections. WT and PBS also sit on different slides, so part of the difference could be slide. The direction held up later, though. Within-section contrasts in §67 found a clear plaque-niche DAM and PIG response in AD sections compared with WT. The overview in §71 rates the AD disease response as robust, because it appears within sections and on WT's own slide. **The disease signal is real, but this run's p-value is not the evidence for it.**

6.how: The input was the spot-level object from §3 with log-normalised expression. Spots were split into two comparisons: PBS against WT, and BRICHOS against WT. For each, Scanpy ran a Wilcoxon rank-sum test per gene. This test asks whether a gene's values in one group's spots tend to be higher than in the other's. Genes with an absolute log2 fold change of 5 or more were removed as likely artefacts. Genes were called significant at false discovery rate (FDR) below 0.05 and absolute log2 fold change above 1. FDR adjusts p-values for testing thousands of genes at once. Volcano plots show fold change against significance and label the top genes. A flag marked significant genes that are on the plaque-induced gene list. There was no control for section or slide. Spots were treated as independent replicates. With a single WT section, any quirk of that one section looks like a disease effect.
6.results: The run produced volcano plots and styled tables but saved neither the tables nor gene counts as text. The one count available comes from §7, which reused the PBS-vs-WT table. There, 143 genes pass FDR below 0.05 and log2 fold change above 1. No count is recorded for the BRICHOS-vs-WT volcano. These p-values are strongly inflated. Spots from the same section are not independent, and the WT group is a single section. The contrast is also confounded with slide, because WT is on P24215 and all PBS sections are on P28052. So the 143 genes mix disease biology with section and slide differences. The run is useful only as a first look at which genes move. Later section-level pseudobulk models (§20, §23) found a DAM and plaque-gene signature with sections as replicates. Nothing from this run was written to the results folder.

7.how: The input was three spot-level Wilcoxon tables from the same notebook. They were PBS vs WT, BRICHOS vs WT, and a third meant to be BRICHOS vs PBS. The aim was to find disease genes that BRICHOS pushes back toward WT. Disease-up genes had PBS-vs-WT log2 fold change above 1 and FDR below 0.05. For each, delta was the PBS-vs-WT fold change minus the BRICHOS-vs-WT fold change. A positive delta means BRICHOS sits closer to WT. A "strict" rescue needed delta of at least 0.5. It also needed BRICHOS significantly below PBS by at least 0.5 log2 units. A "partial" rescue needed only the delta. A second check intersected plaque-induced gene names with the BRICHOS-vs-PBS table. Spots were the replicates, with no slide control. The key flaw is that the third table was computed as PBS against BRICHOS, so its sign is reversed.
7.results: There were 143 disease-up genes. The original run called 0 strict rescues, 24 partial rescues and 119 not rescued. The top partial-rescue genes by delta were Pmch (4.99), Pomc (1.94), Fmo2 (1.59), H2-Aa (1.09), Gbp5 (0.96) and Cd74 (0.93). **The zero was an artefact of a sign error.** The table labelled BRICHOS vs PBS actually held PBS vs BRICHOS, so a positive value meant PBS was higher. The strict rule demanded a value of -0.5 or less, which could only select genes that BRICHOS raises. The code was fixed on 2026-10-23 but not yet rerun, because the data volume was offline. Reading the printed table with the sign flipped, all 20 printed partial genes pass the strict rule. So at least 20 of the 24 are strict rescues at spot level. These genes are not convincing evidence of treatment, though. Pmch and Pomc are hypothalamic neuropeptides, which later work attributes to cutting-plane differences between sections. The MHC-II genes (H2-Aa, H2-Ab1, H2-Eb1, Cd74) are a more plausible lead. Every spot counts as a replicate here, and treatment is confounded with slide. The plaque-gene overlap printout listed 23 of 25 genes but used no significance filter.

8.how: The input was the region-annotated object from §4: 25,660 spots and 18,751 genes. The manual labels were partial, so a uniform region label was needed for all ten sections. Leiden clustering, which groups spots with similar expression, was rerun at nine resolutions from 0.1 to 2.5. Higher resolution gives more, smaller clusters. Marker genes were found for resolution 0.3 by t-test and for resolution 0.75 by Wilcoxon test. The top 20 genes per cluster were printed. The 13 clusters at resolution 0.3 were then mapped by eye to ten named regions. For example, clusters 0 and 11 became caudoputamen and cluster 7 became meninges. PIG (52-gene) and oligodendrocyte scores were dotplotted by treatment and by fine cluster. The check was anatomical coherence. If clusters were driven by noise or slide, their marker genes would not match known brain regions.
8.results: The run produced ten region labels covering every spot. They are caudoputamen, supragranular layers, infragranular layers, hypothalamus, corpus callosum, olfactory areas, meninges, hippocampal formation, thalamus and ventricular area. Markers at resolution 0.75 were anatomically sensible. One cluster was striatal (Rasd2, Ppp1r1b, Drd2) and one astrocytic (Apoe, Clu, Gfap). Others were oligodendrocyte (Mbp, Plp1, Mobp), hypothalamic (Pmch, Hcrt) and thalamic (Prkcd, Tcf7l2). The labelled object was saved and used by every later regional analysis. The module dotplots are images only. Several problems were noted. These regions are expression clusters, not registrations to a brain atlas. A cluster called meninges or ventricular area can mix tissue types, and its makeup can differ by section. The clusters were built on an uncorrected joint embedding, so slide differences could shape the boundaries. The mapping to anatomy was done by eye. "Supragranular" is misspelled in the code, and later file names inherit the typo.

9.how: The input was the spot-level object from §8, with each spot labelled by region and treatment. This was the first test of the core question. Where is the disease signature strongest, and does BRICHOS lower it region by region? A PIG module score was computed per spot. It is the average expression of plaque-induced genes minus that of matched random genes. An oligodendrocyte score was computed the same way. Scores were averaged over all spots in each region and treatment group. The notebook then computed PBS minus WT, the disease increase, and BRICHOS minus PBS, the treatment change. Extra plots included dotplots by region and spatial maps of the scores and of Cst7. There were also spot-level t-test volcanoes of PBS vs BRICHOS in meninges and corpus callosum. No statistical test was attached to the regional means. No unit of replication was defined, so section-to-section variation was ignored.
9.results: PIG score rose in every region in PBS compared with WT. The biggest increases were in meninges (+0.207), olfactory areas (+0.206) and supragranular cortex (+0.193). The smallest was ventricular area (+0.047). BRICHOS minus PBS was negative in 6 of 10 regions. These were olfactory (-0.044), supragranular (-0.035), thalamus (-0.035), meninges (-0.034), infragranular (-0.027) and caudoputamen (-0.016). That is about 11 to 22% of the disease increase. BRICHOS made almost no difference in hypothalamus and hippocampus. It was higher than PBS in corpus callosum (+0.050) and ventricular area (+0.075). The oligodendrocyte score was higher with BRICHOS in seven regions. These are untested spot means, and the PIG list used is ambiguous because cells ran out of order. Later work weakened the result. Section-centred analysis in §68 kept this regional ranking, but no region reached significance (best p about 0.13). **The only BRICHOS section on the PBS slide, 401, showed the opposite regional profile.**

10.how: The input was only the spots labelled meninges in §8, from all ten sections. Meninges had the highest PIG score in §9. The question was whether BRICHOS dampens individual plaque and glial marker genes there. Scanpy t-tests compared PBS against WT and BRICHOS against WT on log-normalised expression. Results were reported for 18 markers, including Cst7, Tyrobp, Trem2, Gfap, B2m, Fcer1g and the C1q genes. One listed name, "Cab", is not a real gene. Cst7, Tyrobp and Trem2 mark disease-associated microglia (DAM), a microglial state found near amyloid plaques. Gfap marks reactive astrocytes. Wilcoxon rankings for PBS vs BRICHOS were also plotted, plus a bar chart of fold changes for the PIG markers. A per-section pseudobulk count table was built but never tested. Spots were treated as independent, and WT is one section. The p-values are therefore pseudoreplicated.
10.results: Compared with WT, PBS meninges showed strong DAM and astrocyte induction. Log2 fold changes were Cst7 5.11 (adjusted p 3.5e-34), Tyrobp 2.35, Trem2 1.76, Fcer1g 1.71, Gfap 1.60 and B2m 1.24. BRICHOS meninges showed almost the same pattern. Their values were Cst7 4.87, Tyrobp 2.28, Trem2 1.62, Gfap 1.57, Fcer1g 1.39 and B2m 0.80. Cst3 did not change in either group. So BRICHOS-treated meninges keep nearly the full plaque response. Only B2m, Fcer1g and Trem2 are somewhat lower than in PBS. This matches the later whole-section finding that BRICHOS does not abolish the DAM signature (§21, §23). Within-section contrasts in §67 also found the plaque-niche response fully present under BRICHOS. The p-values here are inflated by spot-level testing and a single WT section. The meninges label is an expression cluster, not dissected tissue. The pseudobulk table was set up, but no model was fitted to it.

11.how: The input was the processed spot-level object from §3. Chen et al. 2020 ran spatial transcriptomics in an Alzheimer's mouse model and reported six dysregulated genes. Their log fold changes were Cst7 1.91, Cd68 1.70, C1qa 1.04, Slc1a3 0.57, Clu 0.41 and Mbp 0.37. The aim was to see whether the same genes look changed here, as an outside check on the disease model. The notebook drew a dotplot of these six genes by treatment group: WT, PBS and BRICHOS. In a dotplot, dot colour shows mean expression and dot size shows the fraction of spots expressing the gene. Expression was variance-scaled per gene, so colours compare groups within a gene, not across genes. No test was run and no fold changes were computed. So the run cannot say whether effect sizes match the published ones. It also cannot separate disease from slide, since WT and PBS sit on different slides.
11.results: The run produced a single dotplot image. No statistics were computed. No fold changes were calculated, so there is no numeric comparison with the published values. Any agreement with Chen et al. can only be judged by eye from the figure. The catalogue records no reading of the figure. The run is therefore qualitative. It neither confirms nor refutes the published signature. Related numbers come from other runs. The section-level pseudobulk models found Cst7 strongly up in PBS against WT, with log2 fold change 6.85 (§20, §23). Cd68 was up 1.57 and C1qa about 1.03 in §23. Those values are larger than the Chen et al. ones, but models, units and reference animals differ. No later run revisited this comparison directly.

12.how: The input was the spot-level object from §8, using log-normalised expression. BRICHOS is the chaperone domain of the Bri2 and Bri3 proteins, which are encoded by Itm2b and Itm2c. So the first question was whether disease or treatment alters these endogenous genes. Four tight-junction genes were added as blood-brain barrier readouts: Cldn5, Ocln, F11r and Tjp1. Tight junctions seal the gaps between endothelial cells in brain blood vessels. The notebook drew a dotplot by treatment. It then ran Scanpy t-tests on all spots for BRICHOS vs WT, PBS vs WT and BRICHOS vs PBS. Results were reported for the six genes. Spots were treated as independent replicates, with no section or slide term. There was no regional breakdown. With about 25,000 spots, even tiny differences reach significance. Effect size therefore matters more than p-value here.
12.results: Itm2c did not change. Its log2 fold changes were about 0 for BRICHOS vs WT, -0.015 for PBS vs WT and 0.016 for BRICHOS vs PBS, all non-significant. Itm2b rose slightly in both AD groups (0.069 BRICHOS, 0.053 PBS, vs WT), with no BRICHOS-vs-PBS difference. The tight-junction genes shifted in PBS and partly back with BRICHOS. Cldn5 fell in PBS (-0.377) and less in BRICHOS (-0.255). Tjp1, F11r and Ocln rose in PBS (+0.184, +0.385, +0.356). BRICHOS was lower than PBS for all three (-0.185, -0.191, -0.241). Against WT, BRICHOS showed Tjp1 near 0, F11r +0.194 and a non-significant Ocln +0.115. **All effects are small, below 0.4 log2 units.** They are spot-level, slide-confounded and anchored on one WT section. A later section-level signature analysis (§41) found the tight-junction signature mostly moved against rescue across regions. So the partial return seen here did not hold up there.

13.how: The input was the spot-level object from §8. The README asked for gene ontology (GO) analysis focused on endocytosis, after hints of microglial effects in bulk data. GO terms are curated groups of genes that share a biological process. First, Scanpy t-tests on log-normalised spots compared PBS vs WT, BRICHOS vs WT and BRICHOS vs PBS. Three enrichment analyses followed. g:Profiler over-representation asked whether significant up or down genes fall into endocytosis-related terms more often than chance. Those genes had FDR of 0.05 or below and absolute log2 fold change of at least 0.25. GSEA prerank ordered all genes by signed significance for PBS vs WT. It asked whether a term's genes cluster at the top or bottom, using 1,000 permutations. A third g:Profiler run used the top 500 genes by fold change per contrast. Spots were treated as independent, so the significance values feeding the ranking were inflated. No slide control was included.
13.results: For PBS vs WT, no endocytosis-related term reached FDR below 0.3 in the GSEA ranking. The best was Positive Regulation of Endocytosis (normalised enrichment score +1.46, FDR 0.31). Its leading genes were microglial: B2m, Trem2, Mertk, Fcer1g and Cyba. Presynaptic Endocytosis scored -1.73 (FDR 0.32) and Synaptic Vesicle Endocytosis -1.79 (FDR 0.35). The direction was microglial and lysosomal terms up and synaptic vesicle terms down, but nothing was significant. The declared endocytosis prediction therefore failed. 9.49% of ranks were tied, a sign of inflated spot-level p-values. For BRICHOS vs PBS, the most down-regulated genes were Pmch (log2 fold change -4.99) and Hcrt (-4.46). These are hypothalamic neuropeptides, which later notes attribute to cutting-plane differences, not treatment. The most up-regulated genes were zero-count artefacts. Over-representation results exist only as bubble plots. A later section-level analysis (§41) found the endocytosis signature moved against rescue in all seven regions tested.

14.how: The input was raw counts from the spot-level object in §8. Counts were pseudobulked: all spots of one Leiden cluster in one section were summed into one profile. This gave 130 section-by-cluster profiles, of which 91 came from WT or PBS sections. DESeq2, via pydeseq2, then tested PBS against WT for all 18,751 genes with treatment as the only factor. DESeq2 fits a negative binomial model that estimates fold changes while handling count noise and library size. The filtering calls in the notebook only drew plots, so no genes were removed. Cluster was not in the model. Each gene's Wald statistic was scored with decoupler's univariate linear model (ULM). ULM asks whether a set's genes have higher or lower statistics than other genes. Three resources were used: CollecTRI transcription factor targets, PROGENy pathway response genes and MSigDB Hallmark sets. No control or replication check was run.
14.results: DESeq2 warned that iterative size-factor fitting did not converge, because every gene had at least one zero. The number of significant genes was not printed. Some very low-count olfactory receptor genes came out highly significant, for example Olfr881 with mean count 0.005. Transcription factor scoring found 87 significant factors. They included Cebpa (+4.51), Cebpd (+4.36), Stat5a (+4.41) and Trp53 (-3.78). PROGENy pathways in PBS vs WT were NF-kB +17.35, hypoxia +12.20, p53 +12.17 and TNF-alpha +12.06. VEGF (-5.66), PI3K (-3.97) and TGF-beta (-3.07) were lower. Thirty Hallmark sets were significant, led by oxidative phosphorylation (-10.45) and DNA repair (-8.03). Allograft rejection was up (+7.22). These scores fit an inflammatory disease state. However, the 13 WT profiles all come from one section, so the profiles are pseudoreplicates. Cluster was not modelled, nothing was filtered and the contrast is slide-confounded. §15 shows that BRICHOS vs WT gives almost the same profile.

15.how: This run repeated §14 for the treated animals. Spots from PBS sections were removed first, leaving the WT section and the three BRICHOS sections. Raw counts were summed per section and Leiden cluster. The catalogue reports 48 profiles from 4 sections; the notebook does not print this count. pydeseq2 fitted a model with treatment as the only factor and tested BRICHOS against WT. Each gene's Wald statistic was scored with decoupler ULM. The resources were CollecTRI transcription factor targets, PROGENy pathways and MSigDB Hallmark sets, kept at adjusted p below 0.05. The logic was a comparison of two profiles. If BRICHOS reversed the disease programme, inflammatory pathways should be weaker here than in PBS vs WT. No interaction test compared the two runs formally. The slide structure also differs. WT and two BRICHOS sections share slide P24215, whereas in §14 all PBS sections sat on P28052.
15.results: Size-factor fitting again did not converge. There were 103 significant transcription factors, for example Cebpa +4.72, Cebpd +4.80 and Trp53 -3.83. PROGENy pathways were NF-kB +18.53, hypoxia +13.13, p53 +12.94, TNF-alpha +12.82 and EGFR +11.02. VEGF (-6.43), PI3K (-3.67) and TGF-beta (-2.99) were lower. Thirty-three Hallmark sets were significant, including DNA repair (-8.21) and allograft rejection (+6.22). **Every PROGENy pathway had the same sign as in PBS vs WT, with similar or larger size.** For example NF-kB was 18.5 here against 17.3 in §14. At this resolution, BRICHOS tissue looks as inflamed as PBS tissue relative to WT. That argues against a broad reversal of pathway activity. The comparison is descriptive only. It shares the flaws of §14: pseudoreplicated cluster profiles, one WT section, no filtering and non-converged size factors. Later whole-section models (§21, §23) reached the same conclusion with sections as replicates.

16.how: This run was meant to complete the set started in §14 and §15 by testing the treatment contrast itself. The input was raw counts from the spot-level object in §8. Counts were summed per section and Leiden cluster to give 130 profiles. The 117 profiles from PBS and BRICHOS sections were kept, dropping WT. pydeseq2 was set up with treatment as the only factor and a Wald test of BRICHOS against PBS. The planned next steps were a volcano plot and decoupler ULM scoring. As before, the resources were CollecTRI, PROGENy and Hallmark. That would have shown which transcription factors and pathways BRICHOS changes relative to untreated AD. No control or replication check was planned beyond the earlier design. Had it run, every BRICHOS-vs-PBS difference would also carry a slide difference. All PBS sections are on P28052, while two of three BRICHOS sections are on P24215.
16.results: No results exist. The DESeq2 cell shows only partial log output, covering size factors and dispersions, and has no execution count. Every later cell is unexecuted. That includes the results table, volcano, transcription factor scoring and pathway scoring. There are no saved outputs from this notebook. So the run produced nothing that can be interpreted. The problems it would have carried are known from §14 and §15. Section-by-cluster profiles are not independent replicates, and the model has no cluster term. Size-factor fitting struggled in the sister notebooks. On top of that, BRICHOS vs PBS is confounded with slide. The direct treatment contrast was later done at section level in other runs. §17 tested it region by region and found zero significant genes. §23 tested whole sections and found 27, mostly small effects or anatomical genes.

17.how: The input was raw counts from the spot-level object in §8, with the ten cluster-based regions. Counts were pseudobulked: all spots of one region in one section were summed into one profile. So each section counts once per region. A tissue-wide profile per section was added as an extra "region". Every region therefore had ten profiles: 1 WT, 6 PBS and 3 BRICHOS. For each region, pydeseq2 fitted a negative binomial model with condition as the only factor. Wald tests then compared PBS vs WT, BRICHOS vs WT and BRICHOS vs PBS. Genes were significant at FDR below 0.05. Using sections as replicates fixes the spot-level pseudoreplication of earlier runs. A real treatment effect must now beat section-to-section variation, not spot noise. There was still no slide term, because slide and treatment cannot be separated. Mean expression per condition was added, and tables were written to a folder that no longer exists.
17.results: No region had a single BRICHOS-vs-PBS gene at FDR below 0.05. The disease contrasts concentrated in two regions. Ventricular area had 127 genes for PBS vs WT and 50 for BRICHOS vs WT. Thalamus had 24 and 29, and the tissue-wide profile 19 and 6. Corpus callosum had 3 and 0, hypothalamus 1 and 2, and each cortical layer group 1 and 0. Olfactory areas, caudoputamen, meninges and hippocampal formation had none in any contrast. **The partial rescue seen at spot level (§7, §9) does not reach significance with sections as replicates.** This null is not proof of no effect, because 3 BRICHOS sections and 1 WT section give low power. §18 showed that the ventricular and tissue-wide disease signal looks like tissue-makeup differences. The slide confound remains. A similar per-region model in §25 later found 0 to 43 BRICHOS-vs-PBS genes per region. The catalogue does not explain the difference. The output tables are no longer on disk.

18.how: This run used the per-region DESeq2 results from §17. The idea was to see rescue directly. For each region, genes were plotted with their PBS-vs-WT log2 fold change on the x-axis. Their BRICHOS-vs-WT fold change went on the y-axis. A disease-up gene that BRICHOS normalises would fall below the diagonal: up in PBS, closer to zero in BRICHOS. Genes on the diagonal change equally in both groups, which means no rescue. Genes were kept if mean expression was at least 3 counts per million. Points were coloured by the difference between the two fold changes and sized by expression. They were outlined if adjusted p was below 0.05. The top 20 genes per contrast with adjusted p below 0.5 were labelled, a loose threshold. Figures were saved for every region. No formal test of slope or attenuation was done, so the run is descriptive.
18.results: In regions with signal, points lay on or near the diagonal. BRICHOS largely reproduced the PBS-vs-WT changes. In thalamus, DAM and microglial genes rose about equally in both groups. Cst7 had log2 fold change 7.88 in PBS and 8.19 in BRICHOS, Tyrobp 1.93 and 1.90, and Cd52 2.35 and 2.45. In ventricular area, the top genes for both contrasts were neuronal, such as Chgb, Npy, Slc17a7 and Nrgn. That suggests the cluster held different amounts of neuronal tissue in different sections, not plaque biology. Tissue-wide, the top PBS-vs-WT genes were choroid plexus and ependymal genes that were lower in PBS. Examples are Kcnj13 (-1.95), F5 (-2.11) and Aqp1 (-1.82). **Much of the disease signal outside thalamus looks like composition differences between the single WT section and the rest.** In hypothalamus, P2ry12, Ctss and Cx3cr1 were lower in BRICHOS vs WT, but not significantly. All comparisons rest on one WT section and carry the slide confound.

19.how: The goal was cell-type composition per spot, to help interpret regional effects. Two single-cell reference atlases were used: parts of the Allen ABC whole mouse brain atlas and the Linnarsson mouse atlas. A class-balanced reference was built with up to 12,000 cells per class. The seven classes were neurons, oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, vascular, immune, peripheral glia and ependymal cells. scVI, a neural network that learns a compact representation of single-cell counts, was trained on the reference. Then scANVI, a version that also learns cell labels, was trained. A scVI smoke test ran 3 epochs, and scANVI ran 20 epochs. The trained model assigned one hard label to each Visium spot. A logistic regression classifier was started but produced no predictions. A separate notebook tried a cell2location regression model on the Linnarsson reference. That model estimates a reference expression signature per cell class. No validation against known anatomy was run.
19.results: The scANVI labels called 25,333 of 25,660 spots "Neurons". Only 120 were called vascular, 108 ependymal, 74 astrocytes, 24 oligodendrocytes and 1 immune. That is about 99% neurons. **This is a failure, not a finding.** White matter such as the corpus callosum should be dominated by oligodendrocytes, and every region contains glia. A single hard label is also the wrong model for Visium spots. Each spot holds roughly 1 to 10 cells of mixed types. The catalogue also notes that only a few training epochs were run. The cell2location attempt crashed during training with NaN parameter values and produced no output. Neither notebook saved any results. Both were exploratory scratch code. The question was later handled by cell2location and stereoscope deconvolution in notebooks 03/09 to 03/09e. Those methods estimate a mixture of cell types per spot instead of one label.

20.how: This run defined the baseline Alzheimer's model signature before asking whether BRICHOS reverses it. Input was raw counts from the spot-level object in §8, restricted to PBS and WT sections. Counts were pseudobulked: all spots of a section were summed into one profile, so each section counts once. This gave 6 PBS profiles from P28052 and 1 WT profile, P24215_101. pydeseq2 fitted a negative binomial model with condition as the only factor and Cook's outlier refitting. A Wald test compared PBS against WT for 18,751 genes. Genes were significant at adjusted p below 0.05. A volcano plot flagged genes with absolute log2 fold change of at least 1. Using sections as replicates avoids spot-level pseudoreplication. But with one WT section, the variability estimate comes almost entirely from the PBS group. No slide term was possible, because WT and PBS sit on different slides.
20.results: 803 genes were significant at adjusted p below 0.05. The strongest up-regulated genes were microglial and plaque-associated. Cst7 had log2 fold change 6.85 (adjusted p 1.2e-85), Itgax 5.18, Ccl3 5.14, Fgr 3.46 and Ccl6 3.42. Cd74, Ccl4, Pdcd1 and H2-Aa were also up by more than 2. Tyrobp (1.84), Gfap (1.81) and Cd52 (2.07) were highly significant. Cst7, Itgax and Tyrobp mark disease-associated microglia, and Gfap marks reactive astrocytes. So the model shows the expected plaque response. The most down-regulated genes included Calca (-3.27), Crb1 (-2.02) and Ngfr (-1.93). Tables were written to a results folder that no longer exists on disk. The WT-anchored p-values are fragile with one WT section, and disease is confounded with slide. Even so, later within-section contrasts (§67) confirmed the plaque-niche DAM and PIG response. **The overview in §71 rates the AD disease response as robust.**

21.how: This was the treatment arm of the first figure pair. It asked whether the §20 disease signature persists in BRICHOS-treated mice. The pipeline was the same as in §20. Raw counts were restricted to BRICHOS and WT sections and summed per section, so each section counts once. That gave 3 BRICHOS profiles (P24215_201, P24215_301, P28052_401) and 1 WT profile (P24215_101). pydeseq2 fitted a negative binomial model with condition as the only factor. A Wald test compared BRICHOS against WT, with significance at adjusted p below 0.05. If BRICHOS abolished the plaque response, DAM and PIG genes should not be up here. The slide structure differs from §20. Two of three BRICHOS sections share slide P24215 with WT. This contrast is therefore less slide-confounded than PBS vs WT. It also means the two significant-gene counts are not directly comparable.
21.results: 46 genes were significant at adjusted p below 0.05, against 803 in §20. The top up-regulated genes were again microglial and plaque genes. Cst7 had log2 fold change 6.72 (p 6.2e-70), Itgax 5.39, Ccl3 4.88, Ccl6 3.30 and Cxcl5 2.85. Cd52 (1.98), Tyrobp (1.88), Gfap (1.67), Cd68, C3ar1 and Trem2 (1.54) were also up. The C1q genes rose by about 1.0 to 1.1. These fold changes are close to those in PBS vs WT. **BRICHOS does not abolish the plaque and DAM response.** The smaller gene count mostly reflects fewer replicates, 3 against 6, so it is not evidence of rescue. The different slide structure of the two contrasts also affects the counts. Tables were written to a folder that no longer exists. Later runs agree. §22 and §23 found nearly identical BRICHOS and PBS fold changes for disease markers. §67 found the plaque-niche response fully present under BRICHOS within sections.

22.how: This was a quick way to look for genes that BRICHOS modulates differently from PBS. It used the significant-gene tables from §20 (803 genes) and §21 (46 genes). Both were measured against the same WT section. No new model was fitted. For shared genes, the PBS-vs-WT log2 fold change was plotted against the BRICHOS-vs-WT fold change. Delta was the BRICHOS fold change minus the PBS fold change. Genes with an absolute delta of at least 0.2 were coloured. A gene on the diagonal changes equally in both groups. A disease-up gene below the diagonal would suggest BRICHOS weakens its induction. The table holding these columns is not created anywhere in the saved notebook. The plot therefore depended on hidden state in the running session. No test or uncertainty was attached to the deltas. Because both tables share one WT section, delta effectively compares BRICHOS with PBS, slide difference included.
22.results: No numbers were printed. In the saved figure, nearly all plotted genes lie close to the identity line. Disease genes changed by about the same amount with or without BRICHOS. Only four genes pass the 0.2 delta threshold. Itgax and Thbs4 are higher under BRICHOS, while Ccl3 and C4b are lower. These were read from the figure, not from printed output. Cst7 sits on the diagonal, at 6.85 in PBS and 6.72 in BRICHOS. So this run gives no sign of broad rescue. The notebook cannot be reproduced as saved, because the comparison table is undefined. The figure manifest labels the exported image "Volcano: BRICHOS vs PBS", but it is actually this delta scatter. The figure shows only shared significant genes, all of them up-regulated. §23 replaced this approach with a joint model that tests BRICHOS against PBS directly.

23.how: Runs §20 to §22 fitted the groups separately. This run fitted WT, PBS and BRICHOS together in one model. All ten sections were pseudobulked, so each section counts once. pydeseq2 fitted a negative binomial model with condition as the factor and WT as reference. Fitting all groups at once shares the variability estimate across groups. It also lets BRICHOS be compared with PBS directly. Three Wald contrasts were computed: PBS vs WT, BRICHOS vs WT and BRICHOS vs PBS. Significance was adjusted p below 0.05. The run correlated PBS-vs-WT and BRICHOS-vs-WT fold changes across all genes. It checked core marker genes and plotted BRICHOS-vs-PBS fold change against disease fold change. For the 53 plaque-induced genes found in the data, it compared the two WT-anchored fold changes. The BRICHOS-vs-PBS contrast is confounded with slide, because all PBS sections are on P28052.
23.results: The model found 382 significant genes for PBS vs WT, 170 for BRICHOS vs WT and 27 for BRICHOS vs PBS. The two disease fold-change profiles correlated strongly across genes (r = 0.81). Core disease markers were not reversed. Cst7 was up 6.85 in PBS vs WT but changed only -0.13 between BRICHOS and PBS. Gfap went from 1.81 to -0.13, Trem2 from 1.63 to -0.09, C1qa from 1.03 to -0.04 and Cd68 from 1.57 to +0.03. The 27 BRICHOS-vs-PBS genes were mostly small effects, such as Insig2 (+0.21) and Hdgfl2 (-0.23). The larger ones were Gh (-1.53) and Pomc (-2.02), pituitary and hypothalamic hormone genes. They probably reflect how much of those tissues each section captured. Apoe did not change (PBS vs WT 0.13, adjusted p 0.50). **At whole-section level BRICHOS barely moves the disease signature.** Counts of attenuated PIGs were not printed. The similar tissue-wide model in §17 gave only 19 PBS-vs-WT genes, which the catalogue does not reconcile.

24.how: The question was whether a plaque-gene score differs between BRICHOS and PBS within each brain region. Regions were the ten cluster-based compartments from §8. The plaque score was each spot's mean log-normalised expression of 53 plaque-induced genes, over 25,660 spots. Five tests were run. A spot-level mixed model fitted score against treatment, region and their interaction, with a random intercept per section. A random intercept gives each section its own baseline, so spots of one section are not treated as independent. Spot-level Mann-Whitney tests and a two-way ANOVA were also run, and these do treat spots as independent. Next, spot scores were averaged per section and region. A one-way ANOVA compared WT, PBS and BRICHOS section means. Finally, a Mann-Whitney test compared 6 PBS with 3 BRICHOS sections per region, with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction. That last test is the appropriate one, because the section is the replicate.
24.results: In the section-level test, BRICHOS was lower than PBS in 7 of 9 regions. The clearest were infragranular cortex (difference -0.029, p 0.024) and supragranular cortex (-0.039, p 0.024). Both had FDR 0.107, so neither survives correction. Caudoputamen followed (-0.028, p 0.095). The other regions had p of 0.17 or more, and thalamus dropped out of this test. With 6 against 3 sections, 0.024 is the smallest two-sided p this test can give. Spot-level tests gave p below 0.05 in every region, which is pseudoreplication. The section ANOVA was significant in cortex, but it includes WT and so mixes in the disease difference. The mixed model gave a PBS-vs-BRICHOS effect of +0.033 (p 0.20), with fitting warnings. An earlier buggy cell exported a manuscript panel showing "FDR=nan". The score is also sensitive to spot depth. After later slide removal, infragranular rescue reached p 0.012 (§69). **That rescue rests on the P24215 BRICHOS sections, and section 401 alone does not replicate it.**

25.how: The input was raw spot counts from all ten sections, with each spot assigned to one of ten brain regions. Counts were summed per section and region into "pseudobulk" profiles: one sample per section per region, so spots are not treated as independent replicates. Within each region, pyDESeq2 fitted a model with treatment as the only factor across WT, PBS and BRICHOS. DESeq2 models each gene's counts and tests whether its log2 fold change (LFC) between two groups differs from zero. P-values were adjusted for multiple testing (padj, Benjamini-Hochberg). Genes were called differentially expressed (DEGs) at padj below 0.05 for BRICHOS vs PBS. Each region's DEGs were then checked against the 53-gene plaque-induced gene (PIG) list, the core Alzheimer's plaque response. A heatmap showed PIG fold changes per region, and spot-level t-tests ranked marker genes per treatment. An attempted region by treatment interaction model was meant to test whether the treatment effect differs between regions. No control was run. There was no slide term and no label permutation, so a slide difference between PBS and BRICHOS sections could produce DEGs on its own.
25.results: BRICHOS vs PBS gave 43 DEGs in infragranular layers, 40 in supragranular layers, 38 in hypothalamus, 32 in thalamus and 21 in caudoputamen. Most cortical and striatal DEGs were up under BRICHOS, for example 40 of 43 in infragranular layers. Corpus callosum, hippocampus, meninges, olfactory areas and ventricular area had zero DEGs. At most one PIG per region was significant, in caudoputamen, thalamus and supragranular layers. The mean PIG fold change leaned slightly downward under BRICHOS in most regions. It ranged from −0.32 in meninges and −0.26 in olfactory areas to +0.20 in corpus callosum. At spot level, BRICHOS spots ranked Egr1, Faim2 and Syt1 highest, while PBS spots ranked Pmch, Gfap and Cd74 highest. Pmch is a hypothalamic gene, so its appearance as a PBS marker everywhere points to section differences, not regional biology. The interaction model never ran, because only additive terms were specified. These counts rest on 6 PBS vs 3 BRICHOS sections, and all PBS sections share one Visium slide. The DEG counts may therefore be **largely slide batch**, and were never re-checked for it. The single WT section also makes the WT contrasts unreliable.

26.how: The input was section-level pseudobulk: all spots of a section summed into one profile, ten samples in total. A three-group pyDESeq2 model with WT as reference gave each gene's PBS-vs-WT and BRICHOS-vs-WT log2 fold change (LFC). "Disease genes" were those with padj below 0.05 for PBS vs WT. For each disease gene, Δ was BRICHOS-vs-WT LFC minus PBS-vs-WT LFC. A negative Δ for a disease-up gene means BRICHOS sits closer to WT, which this run calls "attenuation". Genes were ranked by Δ to list the 20 most attenuated and the 20 most restored disease-down genes. Bars were coloured by membership of the 53-gene plaque-induced gene (PIG) list. A BRICHOS-vs-PBS volcano plot, filtered by expression and fold change, gave the direct test. No control was applied. The ranking uses point estimates, so it cannot separate a real shift from noise across 3 vs 6 sections. The direct BRICHOS-vs-PBS padj is the only check on each gene.
26.results: The most attenuated genes were H2-Aa (Δ −0.81), Gbp5 (−0.80), Cd74 (−0.72), Zbp1 (−0.60) and Galnt15 (−0.60). Nlrc5, Cybb, Tap1 and Psmb9 followed at about −0.4. Together these point to an **interferon and antigen-presentation axis**, not the core plaque-induced genes. Only H2-Aa among the top 20 is on the PIG list. In the direct BRICHOS-vs-PBS test only Gbp5 was significant (padj 0.020). Adgrl4 reached padj 0.11, and the rest had padj 0.19 to 0.77. The disease-down genes restored most were Calca (+0.82), Ngfr (+0.70) and Anxa8 (+0.58). So the attenuation pattern is a ranking of small, mostly non-significant shifts. The analysis inherits the single WT section and the slide confound. Several notebook cells errored, and one hard-coded gene name is misspelt. Later work weakened the interferon reading. GSEA in §42 again ranked interferon terms lower under BRICHOS, but that signal fell to non-significance once slide was adjusted.

27.how: This run was meant to ask whether BRICHOS effects are carried by particular cell types, such as microglia. The plan was to load a Visium object annotated by Tangram, a method that maps single-cell reference profiles onto spots. Each spot would get its top Tangram cell-type label. Cell-type composition per section and region would be compared between PBS and BRICHOS with Mann-Whitney tests and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. A plaque-induced gene score would be compared by cell type, treatment and region at section level. Finally, spots in the top quartile of immune or microglia probability would be pseudobulked per region and tested with DESeq2. No controls were planned beyond multiple-testing correction. The code uses a 43-gene PIG list that differs from the 53-gene list used elsewhere.
27.results: The notebook was never run, so it produced no results. It has no executed outputs, and none of the tables or figures it would write exist in the repository. The Tangram-annotated input file is also absent. The code imports a module that does not exist, so it would fail at the immune pseudobulk step. Manuscript Figure 5 was meant to hold these panels. All six of its panels are grey "missing" placeholders. Its plaque-score list also differs from the 53-gene list used elsewhere, so results would not have been comparable. The planned tests were section-level Mann-Whitney tests with 3 vs 6 sections, which carry the slide confound. The cell-type question was answered later with cell2location and stereoscope deconvolution in notebooks 03/09 to 09e, not here.

28.how: The input was spot-level plaque-induced gene (PIG) scores already stored in the data object. The idea was that a peripherally delivered agent might act first near the brain surface. For each section, two distances were computed per spot. One was the distance to the nearest meninges spot. The other was the distance to a tissue-border rim, defined as spots near the convex hull of all spot positions. Binned PIG-versus-distance profiles were averaged per section, then across sections per treatment. The main test was a linear mixed model on 22,703 spots from 9 Alzheimer's model sections (6 PBS, 3 BRICHOS). It predicted PIG score from treatment, log distance to border and their interaction, with a random intercept per section. The random intercept absorbs section-to-section offsets, so spots from one section do not count as independent animals. A treatment by distance interaction would show that BRICHOS changes the surface gradient. Border-zone and interior means were also compared. No permutation or slide control was run.
28.results: There was no surface gradient and no treatment-dependent gradient. In the mixed model, the BRICHOS term was −0.018 (p = 0.23) against a PBS intercept of 0.260. The log-distance term was −0.003 (p = 0.10). The BRICHOS by distance interaction was +0.004 (p = 0.20). The between-section variance was estimated at about zero. Raw zone means were PBS 0.255 interior and 0.251 border, and BRICHOS 0.248 interior and 0.230 border. BRICHOS was slightly lower near the border in raw means, but the model did not support this. The declared prediction of a surface-to-depth gradient therefore failed. There are technical problems. Distances are in Visium array-grid units, yet plots label them µm. The convex hull is a poor stand-in for the real tissue edge in coronal sections with ventricles. The border rim and the meninges cluster overlap only partly. The data path points to a volume that is no longer mounted.

29.how: This is infrastructure so that all coronal sections face the same way in figures. A helper rotates each section's spot coordinates and its tissue images by a per-sample angle, with an optional horizontal flip. The angles live in a YAML table, one row per section. A preview script draws each section with treatment-coloured spots and a centre crosshair to check the result by eye. An apply script writes an "oriented" data object. That oriented object is the declared input of the notebooks/03 attenuation series. A generated notebook repeats the same loop interactively. Rotation uses scipy image rotation counter-clockwise, applied identically to coordinates and images so spots stay on their tissue. The tooling changes only how sections are drawn, not any expression values. There is no statistical test. The only check is visual inspection of the preview grid. Without orientation, panels from different sections can look tilted or mirrored, which makes regional comparisons harder to read.
29.results: The tooling exists, but every angle in the table is 0 and no section is flipped. The oriented object is therefore identical to the unoriented one. The interactive notebook has no executed outputs. The preview image is not on disk. The YAML lists 11 sections, including "P24215_401" under PBS. That section does not exist in the analysed data, which has 10 sections and no PBS on slide P24215. This conflicts with the project-wide section list. The default sample column name also does not match the column used elsewhere (sample_id). Paths point to an unmounted volume. The practical effect is harmless, since no rotation was ever applied. Every notebooks/03 analysis that reads the oriented file therefore sees the original coordinates. The phantom section entry is still worth fixing, because it misstates the design.

30.how: This is infrastructure: a first manuscript figure set built from notebooks/01 outputs, dated 2026-05-05. A script tiles PNG panels exported from notebook HTML pages into six composites. It follows Cell journal style, with Helvetica text, a 174 mm double-column width and SVG plus 300-dpi PNG output. Figure 0 is a drawn study schematic. Figures 1 to 5 cover disease baseline, global rescue, regional heterogeneity, spatial gradient and cell type. Missing input panels are drawn as grey "missing" boxes. The script that exported the notebook panels is not in the repository. Panels carry uppercase labels and use 7 to 9 pt text. Figure 1 draws on §20 and §24, and Figure 2 on §21 to §23 and §26. Figure 3 draws on §23 to §26, Figure 4 on §28 and Figure 5 on §27. No checks were run beyond assembling the panels.
30.results: All six composites exist. Figure 5, on cell types, consists only of placeholders, because its source analysis was never run (§27). Several Figure 3 panel titles do not match their content. "Significant gene ranks" is actually a plaque-score bar chart with FDR shown as nan. "PIG response per region" is the top-attenuated-genes bar chart. "Gene-set heatmap" is a PIG fold-change scatter. The schematic gives the design as one WT, three PBS and three BRICHOS animals. The data, however, hold 6 PBS sections. Because the figures reuse notebook renders, they inherit the single WT section, the slide confound and the FDR=nan panel. Figure 4 shows the null spatial-gradient result of §28. None of the figures includes a slide-aware analysis. They were superseded by the three story figures (§31).

31.how: This is infrastructure: three narrative figures drawn directly from the attenuation tables of notebooks/03. Story 1 shows the design schematic, the top PBS-vs-WT genes and PBS-vs-WT changes of plaque-induced genes (PIG). Story 2 shows three per-region tests of BRICHOS vs PBS. Sign concordance is the fraction of disease genes that BRICHOS moves back toward WT, with a binomial test against one half. The rescue slope regresses the BRICHOS-vs-PBS change on the PBS-vs-WT change across disease genes. A negative slope means BRICHOS moves genes back toward WT, and −1 would be full rescue. The slope panel adds a bootstrap interval and a section-label permutation p from 84 relabelings. The third panel shows per-section fractions of low-PIG "responder" spots with Mann-Whitney p. Story 3 has a cascade diagram, a 21-signature heatmap and GSEA terms. The figures add no new statistics.
31.results: The plotted values cover 7 regions with 3 BRICHOS and 6 PBS sections each. Concordance was 0.82 in infragranular cortex, 0.81 supragranular, 0.79 olfactory, 0.76 meninges and 0.74 caudoputamen. Hypothalamus (0.47) and corpus callosum (0.38) showed no rescue. Slopes ranged from −0.104 in meninges to −0.004 in caudoputamen, all far from −1, so any rescue is partial. Corpus callosum had a positive slope of +0.061, the wrong direction. Only infragranular cortex reached significance in the permutation test (p = 0.012). Responder fractions rose under BRICHOS in infragranular cortex (0.066 to 0.105, p = 0.024), supragranular cortex and caudoputamen (both p = 0.048). The permutation label has a formatting bug that prints "p≤.012" whenever p is at most 0.001. Every contrast is confounded with slide. Later slide-removal work found that **only the infragranular rescue partly survives**, and it rests on the two P24215 BRICHOS sections (§69, §71).

32.how: This is infrastructure: a script writes the attenuation findings into the manuscript draft. It uses python-docx to open the Word draft, strip trailing empty paragraphs and append new text. It adds two Results subsections and a Discussion section. The first claims that three orthogonal tests converge on cortical and striatal rescue. The second claims BRICHOS attenuates an interferon-driven microglia-astrocyte cascade and restores neuronal signalling. The prose mirrors a findings note dated 2026-05-05. The output is written as a separate file, leaving the original draft untouched. The statistics it cites come from the notebooks/03 attenuation tables (§36, §38, §39). Regions with at most two PBS sections, namely hippocampus, thalamus and ventricular area, are described as excluded. No checks were run, and the text was not cross-checked against the result tables.
32.results: The script produces text only. It states sign concordance of 0.78 to 0.85 and section-level Mann-Whitney p of 0.048, 0.024 and 0.048. It reports an infragranular slope permutation p of 0.012, with olfactory and meninges at only 0.12. Corpus callosum and hypothalamus are said to fail all three tests. Several statements disagree with the data. The text says "n = 3 vs n = 7 sections", but the tables have 6 PBS sections. It describes 84 reassignments across seven mice, but 84 corresponds to choosing 3 of 9 sections. It calls the Mann-Whitney tests "per-mouse", although the unit is the section. The concordance range quoted is higher than the 0.74 to 0.82 in the tables. Whether the script was run cannot be verified, since its output sits outside the repository. The text predates the discovery of the slide confound, so its **causal claims need hedging**.

33.how: This is infrastructure for the attenuation analysis. With only one WT section, testing WT differences region by region is not valid. The plan was to define the disease response once on whole tissue, then test BRICHOS vs PBS per region against it. A script uses nbformat to generate seven notebooks for that roadmap. They cover pseudobulk, rescue statistics, a signature mixed model, responder spots, a permutation null, confounder checks and broader signatures. All seven share a header that loads the "oriented" data object from the processing volume. Generating notebooks from one script keeps a shared header, data path and helper functions across the series. The helpers live in utils/attenuation.py, which holds the pseudobulk, fold-change, rescue-slope and concordance functions. No checks are part of this step; each notebook carries its own tests.
33.results: All seven notebooks exist in notebooks/03. Their result tables in results/tables/attenuation feed the story figures (§31) and the manuscript text (§32). The scientific results belong to the individual notebook runs (§34 to §42). The oriented input is identical to the unoriented data, because all rotations are 0 (§29). Regenerating the notebooks would overwrite any manual edits made to them since. The confounder-check notebook, one of the seven, was never run (§40). Several generated notebooks also have no saved outputs, so their numbers are known only from the tracked tables. None of the seven includes a slide term. Slide was addressed only later, in notebooks 03/11 to 03/17. Those later notebooks read the same pseudobulk tables rather than regenerating them. The roadmap itself is sound in design, but its outputs inherit the slide confound.

34.how: The input was the region-annotated spot data with raw integer counts. Spots were summed by section and region into pseudobulk profiles. A pseudobulk profile is one sample per section per region, built by adding the counts of all its spots. Section-region pairs with fewer than 10 spots were dropped; the threshold was relaxed from 20 to keep small regions. This makes the section, not the spot, the unit of replication. Treating thousands of spots as independent would inflate significance. Downstream notebooks call each section a "mouse". Every later attenuation analysis reads this table. The sums were rounded to integers, and gene and region names were kept as in the annotated object. The code lives in utils/attenuation.py, and the notebook skeleton was generated by the §33 script. No statistical checks were run at this step.
34.results: The tracked table holds 80 section-region profiles over about 18,750 genes. There are 3 BRICHOS sections, 6 PBS sections and 1 WT section. Seven regions have all 3 BRICHOS, 6 PBS and 1 WT section. They are caudoputamen, corpus callosum, hypothalamus, both cortical layer groups, meninges and olfactory areas. Hippocampus and thalamus have only 1 BRICHOS and 2 PBS, and ventricular area has 1 and 1. So only seven regions can support a BRICHOS-vs-PBS test. The notebook has no saved outputs. Its code names a region column that does not match the saved region names. So the committed notebook is probably not the exact version that made the table. The README lists 3 PBS animals, but the data hold 6 PBS sections, and whether sections share animals is not documented. All PBS sections sit on slide P28052, and 2 of 3 BRICHOS sections on P24215. This **slide confound** affects every downstream contrast.

35.how: The input was the §34 pseudobulk, summed over regions so each section is one sample. Counts were converted to log2 counts per million (log-CPM) plus one. Each gene was tested PBS (6 sections) against WT (1 section) with a t-test. With one WT section, the PBS replicates supply the variance estimate. The notebook itself states these p-values are inflated and descriptive only. "Disease-up" genes were those with fold change above 0.5 and padj below 0.1, joined with the 52 Chen 2020 plaque-induced genes (PIG). "Disease-down" genes were those with fold change below −0.5 at the same padj. This disease axis is defined once on whole tissue, then used region by region in §36. No control was run. There is no second WT animal to check that the axis reflects disease rather than one animal or one slide.
35.results: Of 16,531 genes tested, 167 were disease-up and 32 disease-down. Joining the data-driven set with the PIG list gave 190 disease-up genes; 29 PIG genes were already in the data-driven set. The strongest increases were Cst7 (log2 fold change 5.37, padj 7.8e-5), Ccl6 (3.06), Cd74 (2.80) and Ccl3 (2.36). Cd52, Itgax and Gfap followed at about 1.8 to 1.9. These are microglial, plaque-associated and astrocytic genes, the expected Alzheimer's model response. Hypothalamic neuropeptides Pmch (2.19) and Hcrt (2.13) also ranked high but had padj around 0.8. They probably reflect the cutting plane rather than disease. The padj values are not valid inference with a single WT section. WT sits on slide P24215 and PBS on P28052, so the axis also contains the slide effect. A correction dated 2026-10-22 adds that the disease axis and the rescue axis share this slide effect with opposite signs. **Slide alone can therefore produce an apparent rescue** in §36. The disease response itself was later judged robust within sections.

36.how: The input was the §34 section-region pseudobulk in log2 counts per million. For each of seven regions with 3 BRICHOS and 6 PBS sections, a Welch t-test gave each gene's BRICHOS-vs-PBS log2 fold change. These were compared with the global PBS-vs-WT disease axis from §35. Sign concordance is the fraction of disease genes BRICHOS moves back toward WT. It was tested against one half with a binomial test, plus a one-sided Wilcoxon test. Rescue slope: regress the BRICHOS-vs-PBS change on the PBS-vs-WT change across the 190 disease-up genes. A negative slope means BRICHOS moves genes back toward WT, and −1 means full rescue. A 95% interval came from 1,000 bootstrap resamples of genes. These checks treat genes as independent, so they test consistency across genes, not across animals. The section-level permutation test that addresses this is §39. No slide control was included.
36.results: Concordance was high in infragranular cortex (0.82), supragranular cortex (0.81), olfactory areas (0.79), meninges (0.76) and caudoputamen (0.74). All five had binomial p below 1e-12. Hypothalamus (0.47, p = 0.84) and corpus callosum (0.38) showed no rescue. Slopes were steepest in meninges (−0.104), olfactory areas (−0.091) and infragranular cortex (−0.070). Their bootstrap intervals excluded zero. Supragranular cortex and caudoputamen had near-zero slopes. Corpus callosum had a positive slope of +0.061 (interval 0.004 to 0.18), meaning BRICHOS moved disease genes further from WT. All slopes are far from −1, so any rescue is partial. A correction dated 2026-10-22 reports that **slide alone mimics a negative slope**. A pure slide contrast between BRICHOS sections gave a PIG slope of −0.10, while the same-slide treatment contrast gave +0.03. Within-section centring kept the regional ranking but no permutation p fell below 0.13. After RUVg slide removal, only the infragranular rescue held at p = 0.012. That rescue rests on the two P24215 BRICHOS sections, and section 401 alone shows the opposite regional profile.

37.how: The input was spot-level gene-set scores from all ten sections. Five scores were computed with scanpy. They were plaque-induced genes (PIG, 52 genes), homeostatic microglia (9) and endocytosis (13). The others were disease-associated microglia (DAM, 20) and activated response microglia (ARM, 14). Each score was modelled with a linear mixed model: treatment, region and their interaction as fixed effects, plus a random intercept per section. The random intercept absorbs section-wide offsets, so spots are not counted as independent animals. WT and caudoputamen were the reference levels. The coefficients therefore compare each treatment with the single WT section. No BRICHOS-vs-PBS contrast was computed. The notebook text describes separate mouse and section effects, but only one grouping was fitted, since mouse equals section here. No slide term was fitted, although the notebook's own notes say to add one.
37.results: All five scores were higher in both PBS and BRICHOS than in WT, each with p below 1e-5. For PIG, PBS was +0.154 and BRICHOS +0.128 above WT in caudoputamen. DAM was +0.089 vs +0.082, ARM +0.089 vs +0.075 and endocytosis +0.091 vs +0.077. The homeostatic score rose about equally (+0.120 vs +0.119), which suggests it partly tracks microglial abundance. So BRICHOS sits only slightly below PBS. For PIG, BRICHOS by region interactions reached p below 0.05 in corpus callosum, meninges, olfactory areas and supragranular layers. A hand calculation from the coefficients put BRICHOS below PBS in caudoputamen, cortex, meninges and olfactory areas. It put BRICHOS above PBS in the other five regions, the same split as §36. The WT coefficients rest on one section that is alone in its random-effect group, so the model is not robust to n = 1. A later slide-adjusted microglial state model (§62) lost significance for the BRICHOS state effects.

38.how: The input was the spot-level plaque-induced gene (PIG) score. Each spot was converted to a z-score against PBS spots of the same region, using their mean and standard deviation. A "responder" was a spot with z below −1, meaning clearly less diseased than typical PBS tissue there. For each section and region, the responder fraction was computed. BRICHOS and PBS sections were compared with a one-sided Mann-Whitney test, with sections as the unit. Using sections keeps the test honest about 3 vs 6 animals rather than thousands of spots. WT responder fractions served as a sanity check, since WT should look least diseased. The nine tests were not corrected for multiple testing. Spatial maps coloured each spot by its z-score to show where responders sit. No slide or depth control was applied.
38.results: BRICHOS had more responder spots than PBS in infragranular cortex (0.105 vs 0.066, p = 0.024). Supragranular cortex (0.170 vs 0.059) and caudoputamen (0.182 vs 0.102) both reached p = 0.048. Hypothalamus, olfactory areas and corpus callosum leaned the same way but were not significant (p 0.19 to 0.36). Meninges went the other way (0.080 vs 0.107, p = 0.87). This contradicts §36, where meninges had the steepest rescue slope. WT spots scored as responders at 0.25 to 0.70 per region, as expected for healthy tissue. The p-values are uncorrected and sit near the smallest values 3 vs 6 sections allow. Figure titles say "relative to regional WT", but the plotted colour is z relative to PBS. The README says "PBS median", while the code uses the mean. Responder status partly tracks lower overall PIG and therefore slide. P24215 sections are shallower in sequencing depth, and nothing here **separates the BRICHOS effect from the slide**.

39.how: The §36 bootstrap and binomial tests resample genes, so they ignore that only 9 sections carry the treatment contrast. This run uses a section-level permutation test instead. WT was held fixed. Every way of labelling 3 of the 9 non-WT sections as "BRICHOS" was enumerated, giving 84 relabelings. For each relabeling and region, the BRICHOS-vs-PBS fold changes were recomputed and the rescue slope refitted. Rescue slope: regress the BRICHOS-vs-PBS change on the PBS-vs-WT change across disease genes; negative means movement back toward WT. The p-value is the fraction of relabelings with a slope at or below the observed one. If the real labels give a slope no steeper than random section groupings, the rescue is not tied to treatment. With 84 relabelings, the smallest possible p is 1/84 = 0.012. Permutation does not break the slide structure, since two real BRICHOS sections are the only non-WT sections on P24215.
39.results: The test was rerun on 2026-10-23 after fixing a gene-set mismatch. Before, the observed slope used 190 genes but the null slopes used only 167, so they were not comparable. With matching genes, only infragranular cortex reaches p < 0.05: observed slope −0.070, null median 0.001, **p = 0.024**. That means 2 of the 84 possible relabellings give a slope at least this steep. The earlier value of 0.012 was the test floor. Olfactory areas (−0.091, p = 0.13) and meninges (−0.104, p = 0.14) have the steepest slopes but are not significant. Hypothalamus (0.26), supragranular cortex (0.32), caudoputamen (0.44) and corpus callosum (0.85) are clearly null. So the steep gene-level slopes in §36 mostly do not hold when sections are the unit. Relabelling sections does not break the slide structure, because two of three BRICHOS sections are alone on slide P24215. The later slide-removal run (§69) uses its own self-consistent permutation test and keeps infragranular cortex significant after RUVg. **Section 401 alone does not replicate** the cortical rescue, so the result rests on the P24215 BRICHOS sections.

40.how: This notebook was designed as four robustness checks a reviewer would request. The first dropped low-quality sections using spot count, median UMI and mitochondrial fraction, then refitted attenuation slopes per region. The second would add slide as a fixed effect, to separate treatment from the Visium slide. The third would regress out deconvolved cell-type fractions, so composition changes are not mistaken for expression changes. The fourth would test whether hippocampal results depend on spots near the meningeal rim. Only the first had code. The slide check was listed but had no code, and the other two skip if their inputs are missing. The composition check needed deconvolved fractions, and the rim check needed a distance-to-rim column. Neither input existed in the data object at the time.
40.results: The notebook was never executed, and its output table does not exist. As written, the quality-control step would produce an empty table. Its fold-change call requires at least two sections per group, and WT has one per region, so every region would be skipped. The planned checks were addressed later in other notebooks. Slide was handled in 03/11 (slide-adjusted microglia state model) and in 03/12 to 03/17 (classifier, within-section contrasts, RUV slide removal and overview). Cell composition was addressed by cell2location deconvolution in notebook 03/09. The meningeal-rim sensitivity check was never done anywhere. No section was ever flagged as low quality, since the list of bad samples was left empty. So none of the four checks contributed to the original rescue claims in §31 and §32.

41.how: The input was the per-region BRICHOS-vs-PBS fold changes from §36, for the seven regions with 3 vs 6 sections. Twenty-one gene signatures were scored. They covered microglial programs, astrocyte states, oligodendrocyte states, vascular cells, neuronal and synaptic genes, and cellular stress. Each gene got an expected disease direction. That came from the PBS-vs-WT disease set (§35) when the gene was in it, otherwise from a signature-level prior. The signed fold change is positive when BRICHOS moves a gene back toward WT. The score per signature and region was the median signed fold change, plus the fraction of genes moving in the rescue direction. Signatures held 7 to 52 genes each. No significance test, null distribution or multiple-testing control was applied. So the map shows direction and size of shifts, not whether they exceed noise.
41.results: In cortex, meninges and olfactory areas, the microglial programs moved toward WT. PIG scored +0.11 to +0.17, DAM +0.05 to +0.23 and MGnD +0.08 to +0.27. Corpus callosum went the other way, with PIG −0.163 and MGnD −0.217. Hypothalamus was also mostly negative, and IRM reached −0.30 there. The A1 astrocyte score rose +0.27 to +0.41 in cortex, meninges, olfactory areas and caudoputamen. Oligodendrocyte stress rose +0.22 to +0.43 in the same regions. Immediate-early plasticity genes scored +0.44 in infragranular and +0.34 in supragranular cortex. Endocytosis moved against rescue in all seven regions (−0.05 to −0.12). These are descriptive medians with no null. The contrast carries the slide confound. The immediate-early "rescue" may be a **depth or handling artefact**, since those genes later drove the treatment classifier. The signature list now holds 23 sets, but the saved table has 21, because the notebook was not re-run.

42.how: The input was the per-region BRICHOS-vs-PBS comparison of §36 in log counts per million, for seven regions. Gene discovery used Welch t-tests per region with adjusted p (padj) below 0.1. Plaque-induced genes were excluded, to find genes outside the known plaque response. The top 30 genes by fold change were annotated with signature membership. Pathway analysis used gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) with gseapy prerank. It ranks all genes by fold change and asks whether a pathway's genes cluster at the top or bottom. The normalised enrichment score (NES) is negative when a pathway is lower under BRICHOS. Pathways came from GO Biological Process 2021. Only nominal GSEA p-values were reported, without FDR q-values. The top 20 terms per region were kept. No slide control was applied.
42.results: Only 6 genes passed padj below 0.1 across all regions, and none belongs to any signature. They were Dvl3 and Canx in caudoputamen, Abra in corpus callosum, Slc25a47 in hypothalamus, and Kif1bp and Cab39 in supragranular cortex. All are small effects with no clear biology. With 3 vs 6 sections, gene-level testing is essentially powerless. GSEA ranked interferon responses lower under BRICHOS in cortex, olfactory areas and meninges. Response to interferon-gamma had NES −2.37 in supragranular, −2.22 in infragranular, −2.06 in olfactory and −1.85 in meninges. Defense response to virus and innate immune response also scored lower in supragranular cortex. Corpus callosum went the opposite way, with inflammatory and defense terms higher under BRICHOS (NES about +2.1). Most top terms sat at nominal p = 0.001, the permutation floor. Both analyses carry the slide confound. Hypothalamic neuropeptides and slide drove treatment separation in 03/12, which likely affects the caudoputamen and hypothalamus terms. The **interferon calming faded to non-significance** once slide was adjusted in the inflammation thread.

43.how: Rexach et al. 2024 describe BA4_MIC-7, a microglial state in human motor cortex read as protective. Its top marker is ITM2B, which encodes Bri2, the precursor of the BRICHOS domain given to these mice. The planned test asked whether BRICHOS shifts spots toward this program. Rexach up-genes (padj below 0.05) were mapped from human to mouse, giving 18 genes, and a 13-gene "core" without likely contaminants. Three smaller sub-signatures and a microglia-content proxy were also defined. The plan included Itm2b fold changes per region and median BRICHOS-vs-PBS signature shifts with a Wilcoxon test. A mixed model would adjust for microglia content, with a random intercept per section. That adjustment rules out a shift that only reflects more microglia. Overlap and correlation with PIG and DAM would check that the signal is not simply the plaque response.
43.results: There is no result, because the notebook was never executed. None of its output tables or figures exist on disk. A memory note says it was not run because the processing volume was unmounted. The Rexach source table lists 3,134 tested genes, with 17 up and 33 down at padj below 0.05. ITM2B is the top up-gene there, with a fold change of 0.74. One indirect number exists. In the §35 disease table, Itm2b does not change between PBS and WT (log2 fold change −0.012, padj 0.97). Notebook 09b claims its result "dovetails" with a BA4_MIC-7 result, but no such result exists. The Rexach sets were added to the signature list, but the broader-signature notebook was not re-run, so they are absent from §41 too. Any future run would be a hypothesis-generating port of a human single-nucleus state onto 55 µm mouse spots. It would also inherit the treatment and slide confound.

44.how: This was the first attempt to estimate cell-type composition per spot. Tangram maps single-cell reference profiles onto spatial spots by learning how reference cells fit each spot. It was run in cluster mode with two references. One was the Linnarsson adolescent mouse nervous system atlas, with 160,796 cells in 7 classes, 16,562 training genes and 300 epochs. The other was an Allen ABC atlas subset from midbrain only, with 29,878 cells in 26 classes and 857 training genes. Both were normalised and log-transformed. Each spot's predicted cell-type scores were rescaled to sum to one, and the top type was called. The work sits in notebooks/00/tangram; its run date is not recorded. No validation was run. The only check was whether calls looked anatomically plausible.
